newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Russia's Lebed sidesteps NATO enlargement row.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed sidesteps NATO enlargement row.

text.p: Russian security tsar Alexander Lebed, who ends his first visit to the West on Wednesday, has carefully avoided a row with NATO over its plans for eastwards expansion while holding out the prospect of ever-closer ties.

The outspoken Lebed, whose two-day visit to NATO's political and military headquarters was discreetly opposed by some member states, still drove home Moscow's message that it was opposed to moves to grant NATO membership to its former satellites.
Lebed, emerging as a strong candidate to replace an ailing President Boris Yeltsin, called for enlargement to be put on hold for a generation to allow the bitter memories of the Cold War to fade.
At the same time, he accepted Russia had no right to veto it, and stressed the need to build on existing cooperation in Bosnia and other areas.
"It was clever, Moscow is saying go ahead: but first ask yourselves, who is more important?," said one independent alliance source.
NATO has said it plans to name countries next year with which it intends to open membership talks with Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic leading the field.

Alliance diplomats praised Lebed's performance, saying he had enhanced his reputation as heavyweight politician. But behind the pleasant declarations and smiling faces there had been no real change of substance, they said.
"There is a certain double-talk from Moscow at the moment, but often in diplomacy presentation is more important than fact. Lebed's presentation was moderate," said one NATO ambassador.
Lebed clearly relished his debut on the world political stage.

A reserve general, he emerged from NATO's military nerve centre in southern Belgium on Tuesday, praising the alliance and pledging closer co-operation. He described NATO's command centre as an "efficient, well-tuned military machine".
Lebed earlier inspected an honour guard of allied soldiers with Supreme Allied Commander Europe, U.S. General George Joulwan, before touring SHAPE headquarters.
The sprawling military headquarters would have played a major part in directing any military operations against the now disbanded Warsaw Pact which Lebed served through most of his career.
"We spoke as two soldiers," Lebed said after emerging into the sunshine from the central control building known as Live Oak. "We talked as two paratroopers."

Lebed said Russia would participate in any new alliance-led mission in Bosnia after the mandate of the current mission runs out in December and said he wanted closer cooperation in NATO's Partnership for Peace (PfP) programme.

Russia has some 2,000 troops in the peace mission in Bosnia, but has made little effort to move ahead with projects Implementation Force (IFOR) in Bosnia and a liaison officer at the military headquarters at Mons.
But Russia has made little effort to move ahead with other projects foreseen in PfP which Moscow agreed to join last year.

"I concluded that the country I have the honour to represent has by no means exploited the full opportunities presented by PFP... I am sure that in the near future we will be able to organise close cooperation," he said.
